Family Health

Changed vaginal odour: gentle care and when to get checked

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A vagina has a natural scent, and it does not need to smell like perfume or have no smell at all. A new, strong or persistent change deserves attention, especially with discharge, itching or pain. The useful question is what has changed and whether treatment is needed, rather than how to cover the smell. Extra washing and fragranced products can make irritation worse.

Natural scent and changes that deserve attention

Normal vaginal fluid helps keep the vagina moist and clean. Its amount and texture can change with the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, contraception and sexual activity. Sweat from the surrounding skin, menstrual blood and semen can also temporarily affect the scent. There is no single approved smell that everyone should aim for.

A pronounced new or persistent smell, particularly with changed discharge, burning, soreness, urinary pain, sores or bleeding, should be assessed. Discharge is not abnormal just because it exists, and clear or white discharge does not rule out every problem. Smell or colour alone cannot identify an infection, establish an STI or measure fertility.

When to seek care promptly or immediately

Arrange a clinician or sexual health assessment for a persistent or worsening change, troublesome itching, burning, unusual discharge or bleeding after sex. Do not spend a week trying home products before seeking help. Pelvic pain with abnormal discharge or possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment. Pelvic or abdominal pain that is severe or worsening, or pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty requires immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

In pregnancy, contact your maternity team about an unusual smell or discharge; any bleeding or suspected leaking waters needs immediate contact with your maternity team rather than a home smell test. After birth, loss or another recent procedure, bad-smelling discharge, fever or worsening lower abdominal pain needs urgent clinical advice now. If very unwell, faint, confused, breathless or bleeding heavily, seek emergency care. A retained tampon with fever, rash, dizziness or other systemic illness also needs emergency assessment.

Possible causes: not all odours are yeast

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a change in the vaginal bacterial balance and can cause a fishy smell with thin discharge, often more noticeable after sex. It is not a fungal infection and is not classified as a conventional STI, although sexual exchange can contribute to recurrence. Trichomoniasis is an STI that can cause odorous discharge; chlamydia, gonorrhoea and other conditions may cause discharge or associated pain and bleeding. Tests, not scent descriptions, distinguish them.

Thrush often causes itching and soreness with thick discharge and usually no strong smell. Skin irritation, a retained tampon or other object can also cause symptoms. If a tampon is forgotten or cannot be removed easily, seek prompt help; do not use tweezers or another instrument, and do not keep probing. A broken or fragile object needs urgent professional removal. Odour alone does not mean infertility; some untreated infections can affect reproductive health, which is a reason for appropriate testing rather than alarm.

Gentle washing means external care

The vulva is the outside skin and folds around the vaginal opening; the vagina is the internal canal. Wash the external area gently with lukewarm water and your hands, and pat dry. If a mild fragrance-free cleanser is comfortable, keep it external; sensitive or sore skin may do better with a clinician-recommended soap substitute. Do not scrub with a rough cloth or loofah, wash repeatedly or put soap inside the vagina.

Avoid douching, including rinsing inside with plain water. Avoid perfumed soap, scented wipes, deodorants and antiseptic washes. The vagina does not need flushing to remove semen or restore cleanliness after sex. Persistent irritation may need examination for a skin condition, not more cleaning. A product that stings should be stopped and discussed with a clinician or pharmacist.

Underwear, moisture and sex

Choose comfortable, breathable underwear, such as cotton, and clothing that does not rub. Change damp exercise clothes or underwear and wash with a product that does not irritate your skin. These steps can improve comfort, but cotton is not a guaranteed infection treatment and synthetic fabric does not automatically cause disease. The vagina does not need extra oxygen from special clothing to function.

Gentle external washing when needed is enough; there is no requirement to wash internally before or after intercourse. Barrier protection reduces STI risk, but does not prevent every cause of odour. Avoid sex that is painful, and follow infection-specific advice on abstinence and partner treatment. Some prescribed vaginal creams and oil-based products weaken latex barriers, so check the medicine and condom instructions rather than assuming protection is unchanged.

Perfume, essential oils and pH products

Do not use perfume or genital deodorant even outside the vaginal canal: the vulvar skin is sensitive and fragrances may irritate it. Diluting an essential oil does not make it a proven or reliably safe genital treatment. Avoid tea tree oil, other essential oils, herbal mixtures or food inserted into the vagina to remove odour. Masking the smell can delay finding the cause.

A home pH result cannot tell BV from every other cause, and a normal result cannot exclude every infection. Over-the-counter products advertised to rebalance pH are not a universal first treatment. Do not start boric acid, antiseptics or repeated antifungals simply because of a smell. A clinician may prescribe a specific product for a confirmed condition, but that differs from routine self-treatment, especially in pregnancy.

Food, fluids and probiotics

A varied diet and enough fluids support general health, but no food or drink is established as a way to cure vaginal odour or reset vaginal pH. Drinking extra water to make yourself sweat is not a treatment. Yoghurt can be part of your diet if tolerated; it is not a vaginal medicine. Do not insert yoghurt or other foods.

Probiotic supplements and fermented foods are not substitutes for testing or prescribed BV or thrush treatment; results from a particular researched product do not establish that every shop product works. In pregnancy follow food-safety guidance, including avoiding unpasteurised milk and yoghurt. Do not use raw dairy or an unregulated fermented drink as an odour remedy. A balanced diet cannot guarantee that BV or another condition will not recur.

What an appointment and treatment may involve

Tell the clinician when the change began, whether there is pain, itch, bleeding or urinary symptoms, any recent products or medicines, possible pregnancy, tampon use and relevant sexual exposures. With your consent, an examination and vaginal swab or urine tests may be offered. A pH measurement can be one part of assessment; a cervical screening test is not a substitute for testing these symptoms. You can ask for a chaperone and ask to stop an examination.

Treatment follows the cause: antibiotics for diagnosed BV or an STI, antifungals for confirmed or appropriately assessed thrush, removal of a retained object, or a skin-care plan for irritation. Do not share leftover medicines or assume all discharge needs an antifungal. Pregnancy changes the choice: for vaginal thrush, CDC guidance recommends a seven-day topical azole course rather than oral fluconazole. Complete the prescribed course and return if symptoms persist or recur.

Recurrence, partners and realistic prevention

Recurring BV is common and deserves reassessment, not blame or escalating cleansing. Clinicians may discuss longer treatment and triggers. Partner guidance has changed: ACOG's October 2025 update supports considering concurrent treatment for male partners of adults with recurrent symptomatic BV, and shared decisions for first episodes or same-sex partners. Ask your service about current local guidance; do not copy an antibiotic regimen or treat everyone automatically.

For an STI such as trichomoniasis, current partners need clinical treatment and sex should wait until treatment is completed and symptoms have resolved; repeat testing is usually recommended for sexually active women around three months later. Uncomplicated thrush does not routinely require treatment of an asymptomatic partner. Gentle external care and following product instructions may reduce irritation, but cannot guarantee no recurrence. BeMama can help record changes and questions; it cannot diagnose the cause or rule out an emergency.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Arrange clinical assessment for a persistent or worsening odour change, especially with discharge, itching, pain or bleeding; describe the symptoms and products you have used rather than waiting a week on home remedies.

Use gentle external care and stop products that irritate. Avoid douching, perfume, essential oils and routine pH correction; do not share leftover medicines or assume every smell needs an antifungal.

Follow treatment for the diagnosed cause and ask about pregnancy-specific choices, current local partner advice and follow-up if symptoms return. Seek prompt or emergency care for warning signs rather than waiting for products or an app.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record changes, products tried and questions for an appointment. It cannot identify an infection from smell, assess fertility, exclude a retained object or emergency, or replace examination and testing.

When to seek help

Pelvic or abdominal pain that is severe or worsening, or pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty needs emergency care now. Contact maternity immediately for any pregnancy bleeding or suspected leaking waters, and seek urgent advice now for bad-smelling postpartum discharge, fever or worsening pain. A retained tampon with fever, rash, dizziness or systemic illness needs emergency assessment. Do not delay care to try deodorants, pH products or an app. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Natural scent varies. A new strong or persistent change with other symptoms needs assessment, not perfume or repeated washing.
  • Wash gently outside only; avoid douching, deodorants, essential oils and routine pH remedies.
  • Foods, probiotics and cotton underwear are not infection cures. Treatment depends on the actual cause and pregnancy status.
  • Pelvic pain, pregnancy or postpartum warning signs, a retained tampon with systemic symptoms, or severe illness changes the urgency; do not wait for home remedies or an app.

Frequently asked questions

What should I eat to prevent vaginal odour?

No food is proven to prevent or cure all vaginal odour. A varied diet and ordinary hydration support health; yoghurt and probiotics do not replace appropriate testing or treatment. Do not insert foods into the vagina. During pregnancy follow food-safety advice and avoid unpasteurised milk or yoghurt.

How can I reduce irritation and unwanted odour?

Use gentle external care, avoid fragranced products and douching, wear comfortable underwear and change damp clothes. These measures support comfort, not guaranteed infection prevention. Seek assessment for persistent or changed odour, particularly with discharge, pain, itching or bleeding.

Is a little itching normal?

Brief irritation can happen, but persistent, recurrent or troublesome itching should be assessed. It may reflect a skin condition, irritation or infection, and does not automatically mean thrush. Do not keep adding scented products or repeating antifungals without advice.

Which products should I avoid around the vagina?

Avoid scented soap and wipes, deodorants, perfume, antiseptic washes, rough scrubbing and essential oils on genital skin. Do not wash inside the vagina or insert food or unprescribed pH treatments. For sore skin, ask about an appropriate fragrance-free soap substitute.

Does a fishy smell prove BV or an STI?

No. It can suggest BV, but a clinician must consider other causes and tests. BV is bacterial imbalance, not thrush; sexual activity can contribute without proving infidelity. An odour alone cannot establish an STI or infertility.

Do I need to treat my partner?

It depends on the diagnosis. STI partners often need treatment, while asymptomatic partners do not routinely need treatment for uncomplicated thrush. For recurrent symptomatic BV, newer guidance supports discussing concurrent partner treatment in selected circumstances. Let a clinician plan it; do not share medicines.

Should I wait a week for home care to work?

No fixed waiting week is appropriate. Arrange assessment for persistent or worsening symptoms, and seek urgent care for pelvic pain, pregnancy or postpartum warning signs. Pelvic or abdominal pain that is severe or worsening, or pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency help. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

What if I might have forgotten a tampon?

Have it removed promptly. If it does not come out easily or you are unsure, contact a clinician rather than using instruments or repeated probing. A retained object with fever, rash, dizziness, confusion, breathing difficulty or other systemic illness needs emergency assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
